title: Sfiha
subtitle: Levantine open lamb pastries
excerpt: Sfiha are small Levantine flatbreads topped with a spiced raw lamb mixture that cooks into the dough as it bakes. Known as Lebanese pizza in many UK restaurants, they are savoury, slightly aromatic, and best eaten hot from the oven with yoghurt and a squeeze of lemon.
sourceNotes: Sfiha (also sfeeha or lahm bi'ajeen in its Levantine form) originated in Syria and Lebanon and is also strongly associated with the Lebanese diaspora in Brazil. They appear at bakeries and restaurants across Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan.

recipe.freezeNotes: Baked sfiha freeze well. Cool completely and freeze in a single layer before stacking. Reheat in a 200 C oven for 6 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Dough can be made the night before and cold-proved. Prepare the lamb topping fresh on the day.
recipe.temperatureNote: Very hot oven; preheat for at least 20 minutes

content.text: Sfiha are somewhere between a pizza and a flatbread. The dough is yeasted but thin, and the lamb topping is spread raw over the shaped rounds before baking. The high oven heat cooks the meat and dough simultaneously in about 10 minutes.

The lamb mixture must be quite fine in texture for this to work. Processing it briefly in a food processor gives the right result; the mixture should look almost paste-like rather than coarsely minced.
Serve straight from the oven. Roll them up with yoghurt and shredded lettuce as a wrap, or serve flat with lemon wedges alongside.
Mix the flour, yeast, and salt together. Add the olive oil and warm water and mix to a soft dough. Knead for 6 to 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and leave to prove for 45 to 60 minutes until doubled.

Combine all the lamb topping ingredients in a bowl and mix well. The mixture should be slightly loose but hold its shape when spread. Squeeze out excess juice from the diced tomato and grated onion before adding if the mixture looks very wet.

Preheat the oven to 230 C. Divide the dough into 8 equal balls. Roll each into a thin round about 15 cm across. Place on lightly oiled baking sheets. Spread a thin, even layer of lamb mixture over each round, right to the edge. Bake in batches for 8 to 10 minutes until the edges of the dough are golden and the lamb is cooked through. Serve immediately.

rows.symptom: Lamb topping too wet and sliding off
rows.cause: Tomato or onion not squeezed dry
rows.fix: Squeeze the diced tomato and grated onion in a tea towel to remove as much moisture as possible before mixing.
Roll to about 3 mm. The thin base is what makes sfiha work; thick dough stays doughy in the centre.

rows.symptom: Lamb cooked but still pale pink
rows.cause: Oven too cool or too much topping
rows.fix: Use a very thin layer of lamb. Too thick a layer cooks unevenly. Ensure the oven is fully preheated.

content.text: Add a pinch of chilli flakes to the lamb mixture for heat. Pine nuts can be pressed into the topping before baking. Sfiha are sometimes finished with a drizzle of pomegranate syrup and a scatter of sumac.

Sfiha are best eaten immediately from the oven. They can be baked ahead and reheated in a 200 C oven for 5 minutes but lose some of their crispness. Freeze any leftover baked sfiha as soon as they are cool.

Sfiha are sold at bakeries across Lebanon and Syria. They are also deeply embedded in Brazilian food culture through the large Lebanese diaspora in Brazil, where they are called esfiha and are sold at every corner bakery. In the UK they appear at Lebanese restaurants and are often called Lebanese pizza on menus.
